title: How California's Preliminary Change of Ownership Report Works
content_html:
What the Preliminary Change of Ownership Report Is

If you've bought or sold property in California, you've likely encountered a form called the Preliminary Change of Ownership Report, usually shortened to "PCOR." It's one of those documents that shows up in a stack of closing paperwork without much explanation, yet it plays a real role in how your new property tax bill gets calculated. Understanding what it does — and what happens if it's left out — can save you confusion and unnecessary cost down the road.

The PCOR is a form the county assessor uses to gather basic facts about a real estate transfer: who the buyer and seller are, the sale price, the type of transfer, financing details, and whether the buyer intends to claim an exemption such as the homeowners' exemption. It is distinct from the deed itself — the deed is the legal instrument that actually transfers title, while the PCOR is an informational report that accompanies it to the County Recorder's office.

Why the Form Exists

California reassesses real property for tax purposes when a change in ownership occurs, under the framework established by Proposition 13. When a new deed is recorded, the county assessor needs to know whether that recording represents a reassessable event and, if so, what the new assessed value should be based on. The PCOR is the mechanism by which that information reaches the assessor's office at the same time the deed is recorded, rather than through a separate, slower inquiry process after the fact.

Without this report, assessors would have far less timely information about sale prices and the nature of transfers — details that are central to administering California's property tax system. The form essentially bridges the gap between the public recording of a deed and the assessor's internal valuation process.

Who Is Responsible for Filing It

In a typical sale, the buyer (the new owner) completes and signs the PCOR. In practice, escrow or title companies usually prepare the form as part of the closing package and have the buyer sign it along with the rest of the closing documents. It is then submitted to the County Recorder along with the deed when the deed is recorded.

Some transfers are exempt from reassessment entirely — for example, certain transfers between spouses, or parent-child transfers that qualify under California's current rules. Even when an exemption applies, a PCOR (or a related exemption form) is typically still filed to document the basis for that exemption, so the assessor's office has a record of why the transfer wasn't treated as a reassessable event.

What Information the Form Asks For

While the exact layout can vary slightly by county, the PCOR generally asks for:

  • The names of the buyer(s) and seller(s)
  • The property's address and assessor's parcel number
  • The date of transfer and the type of transfer (sale, gift, inheritance, etc.)
  • The purchase price and terms of financing
  • Whether personal property or manufactured housing was included in the sale
  • Whether the buyer intends to occupy the property as a principal residence, which is relevant to eligibility for the homeowners' exemption

This is informational, not a public negotiation document — but because it is filed with the county, portions of it can become part of the public record tied to the parcel, similar to other recorded documents.

What Happens If the PCOR Isn't Filed

Recording a deed without an accompanying PCOR doesn't stop the transfer from being legally valid, but it does trigger consequences on the tax side. County recorders in California are generally authorized to collect an additional recording fee when a required PCOR is not filed at the time a deed is recorded, since the assessor then has to pursue the ownership and valuation information through other means. The specific fee amount and the rules around it can change and vary by county, so it's worth checking directly with the county assessor's office for current information rather than relying on a figure that may be outdated.

Beyond the fee, failing to file can also delay the assessor's ability to set the new assessed value promptly, which can create downstream confusion about tax bills, especially if a reassessment and a new owner's first tax bill cross paths awkwardly. Filing the PCOR correctly and on time helps keep the transition from the seller's old assessed value to the buyer's new one administratively clean.

How the PCOR Connects to Your Tax Bill

Once the assessor's office processes the PCOR and the recorded deed, it determines whether the transfer is a reassessable change in ownership. If it is, the assessor establishes a new base year value for the property — generally the purchase price, assuming it reflects fair market value — and that new value becomes the foundation for future property tax bills going forward, subject to the annual adjustment limits established under Proposition 13.

This is also the point at which exemptions come into play. If you've indicated on the PCOR that you'll occupy the home as your principal residence, that notation supports your eligibility to file for the homeowners' exemption, which reduces the assessed value subject to tax.

Special Situations: Inherited and Parent-Child Transfers

Transfers between parents and children, and in some cases grandparents and grandchildren, are subject to special rules that have changed significantly in recent years following the passage of Proposition 19. Whether a given inherited property keeps its prior assessed value or gets reassessed to current market value depends on specific conditions, including whether the property becomes the recipient's principal residence and the relative values involved. Because these rules are detailed and carry real financial consequences, anyone navigating an inherited transfer should look closely at how the current law applies to their situation and confirm the details directly with the assessor's office.

A Practical Note for Buyers and Sellers

For most buyers and sellers working with an escrow or title company, the PCOR is handled as a routine part of the closing paperwork — you'll sign it, it gets submitted with the deed, and the process moves forward without you needing to do anything further. The value in understanding the form isn't that you need to manage it yourself; it's knowing what it's for, so that if a question comes up later about your assessed value, an exemption, or a parcel's tax history, you recognize where that information originated.

If something looks off on your first post-purchase tax bill, or you believe your new assessed value doesn't match what was reported on the PCOR, start by contacting the county assessor's office directly — they can walk through how the transfer was processed and correct any discrepancy.
